findings.title: NPE when the aggregate "Clients" resource does not exist
findings.body: In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and immediately passes the result to `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource()` returns `null` in two reachable situations: (a) `supportsAuthorizationSchema()` is false, i.e. the realm still has an admin-permissions client (so `root.realmResourceServer()` is non-null) but `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` was turned off, and (b) the realm's resource server has no resource named `Clients` (e.g. a realm whose FGAP client was created before this PR, see the missing migration). The policy store dereferences `resource.getId()`, so this throws a NullPointerException, and because `canManage/canConfigure/canView/canMapRoles` all go through this method, every admin REST call touching a client would fail with HTTP 500. Add a null check and return `false`.

findings.title: getClientsWithPermission returns the literal "Clients" and never a real client id
findings.body: `getClientsWithPermission()` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` and adds `resource.getName()` to the result. Only the aggregate resource created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` has its type set to `Clients` (`resource.setType(type)`); per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` are created with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and never get a type. Consequently this method (1) can only ever return the string `"Clients"`, which is not a client id, and (2) never returns the ids of clients that actually have a permission granted. Any caller using this set to decide which clients an admin may act on will both miss all legitimately permitted clients and receive a bogus entry. Either set the resource type when creating per-client resources, or resolve the granted clients differently (and exclude the aggregate resource name).

findings.title: canView() ignores the manage scope, breaking "manage implies view" for client scopes/listing
findings.body: `canView()` is implemented as `canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(VIEW)`. Unlike every other place in this class (`canView(ClientModel)` falls back to `canManage(client)`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)` checks VIEW *or* MANAGE) and unlike V1 where the `manage-clients` role implies view, the global `manage` permission does not imply `canView()`. Since `canList()`, `canListClientScopes()`, `canViewClientScopes()` and `requireView()` (not overridden) are all derived from `canView()`, an admin granted only the all-clients `manage` permission is denied listing/viewing realm client scopes (`requireListClientScopes()` → 403) while `canManageClientScopes()` returns true, so the same admin may create and modify client scopes but cannot list them. `canView()` should also consider the `manage` scope.

findings.title: canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException on a runtime (non-admin) code path
findings.body: `canExchangeTo(...)` now throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. This method is not only an admin-console concern: the legacy token-exchange flow calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)` to authorize exchanging to a target client, and `AdminPermissions.management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever the `admin-fine-grained-authz:v2` feature is enabled — independently of whether the legacy FGAP feature is enabled. With both the (legacy) token-exchange feature and FGAP v2 enabled, token-exchange requests will produce an HTTP 500 from the unchecked exception instead of a clean 403 denial. The V1 implementation returned `false` when no resource server/permission existed; this override should do the same (or the caller must be made V2-aware).

findings.title: Listener guard does not protect against V1+V2 both enabled; client removal will fail with 500
findings.body: The removal listener is now only executed when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1) is enabled, presumably because `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. But `management()` (line 67) prefers `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, and the two preview features are not mutually exclusive. When both are enabled, a `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` reaches `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`, which now throws `UnsupportedOperationException` and aborts the client deletion transaction (HTTP 500). The same applies to the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` admin endpoints, which call `clients().isPermissionsEnabled()`/`getPermissions()` after the V1 feature check passes. The guard should select the V1 implementation explicitly (or V2 should no-op instead of throwing) for these legacy operations.

findings.title: No migration for realms whose admin-permissions client already exists
findings.body: `init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms where FGAP v2 was already enabled before this change never receive the newly added `Clients` resource nor the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`). In such realms: creating a Clients permission reaches `getOrCreateResource()` and hits `throw new ModelException("No scopes found.")` (line 108) for the missing scopes, all-clients evaluation silently returns `false` because `resourceStore.findByName(server, "Clients", ...)` is null, and per-client evaluation NPEs on the null aggregate resource (ClientPermissionsV2 line 219). The PR adds no upgrade/migration step to create the missing scopes and resource for existing admin-permissions clients.

findings.title: getResourceName has no handling for the Clients resource type
findings.body: `getResourceName()` translates resource names to human-readable values only for the `Users` resource type ("All users" for the aggregate resource, the username for per-user resources) and otherwise returns `resource.getDisplayName()`. Per-client resources are created in `getOrCreateResource()` without a display name, and the aggregate `Clients` resource has none either, so every Clients permission exposed through the admin REST API/console will report a `null` resource name instead of the client id/clientId or an "All clients" label. The new resource type needs a branch here (resolving the client via `session.clients().getClientById()`), consistent with the Users handling.

findings.title: resolveClient allows permissions to target the admin-permissions client itself
findings.body: `resolveClient()` resolves any client in the realm, including the realm's own admin-permissions (FGAP policy) client and `realm-management`, even though the class already provides `throwExceptionIfAdminPermissionClient()` for exactly this kind of guard and it is not used here. As a result an administrator can create a Clients permission whose resource is the admin-permissions client and grant `manage`/`configure` on it; since the client authorization admin endpoints are gated on being able to manage the owning client, the grantee can then modify or delete all fine-grained admin permission policies — a privilege escalation out of the restricted scope they were given. Target clients that back the FGAP/admin infrastructure should be rejected when resolving the resource.

findings.title: Javadoc for void require* methods says they return true
findings.body: `requireView()` (line 98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 103) are `void`, but the new Javadoc states "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" / "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}". These should follow the convention used for the other require* methods in this file: "Throws ForbiddenException if ... returns {@code false}". As written the contract documented for implementors/callers is wrong.

findings.title: Dead code and unused imports copied from the V1 implementation
findings.body: `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` (line 262) is private and never called, the `logger` field (line 51) is unused, and the imports `org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope`, `ClientModelIdentity`, `DefaultEvaluationContext`, `EvaluationContext` and the static import of `AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE` are unused. This dead code (apparently copied from `ClientPermissions`) suggests token-exchange support was intended but is not implemented, and it will mislead future readers. Remove it (or implement the missing behaviour).

findings.title: New Clients scopes and all-clients fallback combinations are untested
findings.body: The added tests cover `manage`, `configure`, `view`, `map-roles` and `map-roles-composite`, but there is no test for the newly introduced `map-roles-client-scope` scope (`canMapClientScopeRoles`), none for `getClientsWithPermission()` (which, as implemented, cannot return any client id), and none for the combination of an all-clients permission with an unrelated per-client permission — a case where `hasPermission(ClientModel, scope)` stops consulting the aggregate `Clients` resource as soon as a per-client resource exists, so a previously granted all-clients permission silently stops applying to that client. These are exactly the paths most likely to regress.

findings.title: Feature guard stops cleanup of legacy fine-grained permission policies
findings.body: Previously the role/client/group removal listener ran unconditionally and invoked `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)`, which deletes the V1 fine-grained permission policies/resources associated with the removed object. With the new `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` guard, deployments that created V1 FGAP data and later disabled the preview feature will leak orphan policies and resources into the authorization store when the corresponding roles/clients/groups are deleted, leaving the data inconsistent if the feature is re-enabled. If the intent was only to avoid the V2 `UnsupportedOperationException`, the guard should select the V1 management implementation rather than skipping cleanup entirely.
